title: Cloud Network & Data Security
summary: The network isolation and encryption controls specific to a cloud environment, and matching control strength to how sensitive the data actually is.

slides.markdown:
The network controls covered earlier in this area — firewalls, segmentation — have direct cloud equivalents, but the cloud versions are **software-defined constructs**, not physical devices, and that changes both what's possible and what commonly goes wrong.

This topic covers the specific building blocks: security groups and NACLs for network isolation, VPCs for tenant separation, and encryption at rest and in transit for the data itself. The through-line is **matching control strength to data sensitivity** — not every resource needs the same level of protection, but the ones that do need it, need it applied deliberately, not by default assumption.

slides.subTitle: Stateful instance-level vs stateless subnet-level
slides.markdown:
| | Security groups | Network ACLs (NACLs) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Attached to individual instances/resources | Attached to an entire subnet |
| State | Stateful — allow the outbound request, the reply is automatically permitted | Stateless — inbound and outbound rules must each be defined explicitly |
| Rule evaluation | All rules evaluated; the most permissive matching rule applies (no explicit deny in most implementations) | Rules evaluated in order, first match wins, and explicit deny is supported |
| Typical use | Primary day-to-day access control — "this service can reach that service on this port" | A coarser backstop — "block this entire subnet from talking to that entire subnet," or block a known-bad IP range |

Security groups are the cloud equivalent of a host-based firewall; NACLs are the cloud equivalent of a subnet-level, stateless packet filter. In practice, security groups do almost all the real work day to day, and NACLs are reserved for broad, coarse-grained rules that should apply no matter what any individual security group says — a genuine belt-and-suspenders layer, not a redundant one.

A **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** is a logically isolated slice of a cloud provider's network, dedicated to one account or organization — the cloud analogue of segmentation, but software-defined and provisioned in minutes rather than wired by hand.

Inside a VPC, subnets are typically split into **public** (has a route to the internet gateway — for load balancers, bastion hosts) and **private** (no direct route to or from the internet at all — for databases, internal services, anything that has no business being reachable from outside). A resource in a private subnet can still reach the internet *outbound* through a NAT gateway if it genuinely needs to (say, to pull a software update), but nothing on the internet can *initiate* a connection to it.

The design principle mirrors the DMZ pattern from earlier in this area: only what genuinely needs to be internet-facing sits in a public subnet; everything else — especially anything holding data — sits in a private subnet, unreachable from outside by construction, not by hoping a firewall rule is configured correctly.

slides.subTitle: Provider-managed vs customer-managed keys
slides.markdown:
**Encryption at rest** protects data sitting in storage — a disk, a database, a backup — so that someone with access to the underlying physical media (or a stolen disk, in theory) can't read it without the key. Most providers offer this as a near-default option on managed storage.

The meaningful choice is **who holds the encryption key**:

- **Provider-managed keys** — the provider generates, stores, and rotates the key entirely on their side. Simplest to use, but the provider (and anyone who compromises the provider's key management) has access to it.
- **Customer-managed keys (CMK)** — the customer generates and controls the key (often via the provider's key management service, sometimes fully outside it), and can revoke access to it independently of the provider. This adds real operational overhead — you now own key rotation and availability — but it means you can cryptographically cut off access to your own data, including from the provider's own support tooling, in a way provider-managed keys can't.

Regulated data (health records, financial data) frequently requires customer-managed keys specifically because of this independent-control property, not because provider-managed encryption is technically weaker.

slides.sectionTitle: Encryption in transit inside the cloud
slides.subTitle: Not just at the edge
slides.markdown:
It's common to encrypt traffic between the internet and a load balancer (TLS at the edge) and stop there, treating everything inside the cloud provider's own network as implicitly safe. That assumption is exactly the "trusted internal network" idea that segmentation and zero trust both push back against, applied here to data in motion.

Internal traffic — service to service, service to database, service to cache — travels over the provider's shared physical network infrastructure, and while providers do apply their own protections, a customer that wants a guarantee independent of "trust the provider's internal network" needs to encrypt that traffic itself: TLS between internal services (often via mTLS, covered in netsec), and encrypted connections to managed databases rather than defaulting to plaintext internal connections.

The cost/benefit here scales with sensitivity: encrypting every internal hop adds real latency and operational overhead, so this is a case where **matching control strength to data sensitivity** matters directly — end-to-end internal encryption for anything touching regulated or high-value data, and a more relaxed posture where the data genuinely doesn't warrant the overhead.

slides.subTitle: Knowing what needs the strongest controls
slides.markdown:
None of the controls above are free, so applying the strongest version of every one to every piece of data is both wasteful and, paradoxically, worse for security — teams that treat everything as maximally sensitive tend to under-invest in the controls that actually matter for their most sensitive data, because the effort is spread too thin.

**Data classification** is the practice of explicitly tagging data by sensitivity — public, internal, confidential, restricted/regulated — and tying each tier to a specific, mandatory set of controls: restricted data always uses customer-managed keys and private subnets with no public path, confidential data requires encryption at rest and in transit but permits provider-managed keys, public data (marketing assets, a public API's documentation) needs neither.

The interview-relevant point: "we encrypt everything and lock everything down" sounds strong but is often a sign a team hasn't actually classified their data — the strong answer names the tiers and which controls are mandatory at each tier, showing the controls were deliberately matched to risk rather than applied uniformly out of caution.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: the cost of a public database port
slides.markdown:
Automated internet-wide scanning means a database port exposed with an overly broad security group rule is discovered fast — often within minutes to hours, not days — by bots continuously scanning the entire public IP space for open, commonly-exploited ports. This isn't a hypothetical risk that depends on a targeted attacker finding your specific system; it's closer to certain, on a timescale short enough that "we'll fix the rule tomorrow" is a real, material exposure window, not a formality.

This is why a single overly-permissive security group rule on a database — `0.0.0.0/0` on port 5432 or 3306 — shows up so consistently in real breach post-mortems: it's not a sophisticated attack, it's an automated scan finding a door that was left open, often followed by an automated credential-stuffing attempt within the same window.

slides.sectionTitle: Layering security groups, NACLs, and private subnets
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A staff-level answer treats these controls as **independent, overlapping layers**, not redundant duplicates of the same idea. A private subnet already means nothing on the internet can *initiate* a connection to a database inside it — that's a structural guarantee, not a rule that can be misconfigured away like a security group can. A security group then adds fine-grained, per-resource control on top of that structural guarantee — restricting which specific internal services (not just "anything in this subnet") can actually connect. A NACL adds a subnet-wide backstop that survives even if every individual security group in that subnet were somehow misconfigured to be too permissive.

The reason this layering matters in practice: a single misconfigured security group rule is a realistic, common failure — someone widens a rule to debug something and forgets to narrow it back. If the resource is *also* in a private subnet, that misconfiguration is contained to "reachable from elsewhere inside the VPC," not "reachable from the entire internet" — the private subnet placement is what prevents one security-group mistake from becoming a full public exposure.

slides.sectionTitle: A security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 on a database port
slides.markdown:
The pitfall, concretely: a security group rule allowing inbound traffic from `0.0.0.0/0` (any IPv4 address) on a database's port, usually added "temporarily" to debug a connectivity issue from a laptop or a new environment, and never narrowed back down.

As the numbers slide covered, this isn't a slow-burn risk — internet-wide scanners find open database ports on a timescale of minutes to hours, and an unauthenticated or weakly-authenticated database exposed this way is a routine, unsophisticated compromise, not an advanced attack. It shows up constantly in breach post-mortems precisely because it requires no skill to find, only automation.

The fix is procedural as much as technical: never widen a security group rule to `0.0.0.0/0` for anything holding data, even temporarily — scope inbound rules to specific known IP ranges (a VPN's egress range, a bastion host, another security group) instead, and put the database in a private subnet as a structural backstop so that even a mistaken security group rule doesn't translate directly into internet exposure.
